paras: The Elkins street fight and arrest of Dr. Laws was a clash in Elkins, West Virginia, on Saturday night, 14 August 1920, in which a white man fought Dr. Laws, a Black physician. The white man was fined, Laws was then arrested and his office raided, and the local weekly called it "another race war".
According to the Randolph Enterprise of nearby Beverly, it began when young Black men followed young white men from Beverly who had "yaller" girls with them.

A "big fellow", described as "loaded with moonshine", took up the quarrel and had a "scrap" with one of the Black youths, who got away from him. Later the same man, "still hunting trouble", fought Dr. Laws at the John B. Wilt corner. Laws appealed to the Mayor, who came out to disperse the crowd, and the night policeman and Charley Whetsell broke it up. No injuries were reported.

At a hearing on Monday the Mayor fined the white man $15 and costs. Laws was then arrested for fighting; City Hall was "jammed with a crowd" for his Monday-night hearing, and feeling ran so high that the Mayor postponed it to Friday night, with no outcome reported.

At about 2 o'clock on Tuesday night, two city and three state police raided Laws's office on suspicion of a poker game, finding four white men and another Black man with him, along with cards and chips. All were released on their own recognizance for trial Saturday night.

The only coverage found was a set of short items in the local-news column of the Randolph Enterprise on 19 August. The paper opened the item by calling it "Another race war" between "the whites and blacks", traced it to Black youths following white youths with "yaller" girls, and cast the white man as drunk and looking for trouble. It opened its report of the raid with "They are still after Dr. Laws, the colored physician" and closed the fight item by noting "considerable hard feelings" and that "the end is not yet". No account in the Black press or in other white papers was found.
Laws said the white man who assaulted him had a knife, while some of the crowd said Laws had a knife; the Enterprise did not resolve the point.

framing.detail: The Randolph Enterprise opened the item 'Another race war was started in town', blamed the start on Black youths following white youths with 'yaller' girls, but also cast the white man as drunk and 'hunting trouble' and wrote of the raid that 'They are still after Dr. Laws.'
